semantics.note: 'Could sometimes' means past ability here, not a hedge. The scope 'in these regards' and the 'not reliably' qualifier are both kept.

contract.note: A plain reading, varying correct and incorrect outputs during the release window, is fair and ordinary. The evidence covers the seven failure types unevenly.

evidence.note: OpenAI's launch-day disclosure says answers changed with rephrasing and retries, sometimes correct. It is a company statement, but it admits a weakness.
A contemporaneous report of December 2022. Piantadosi says the biased outputs did not appear the same way every time, while direct prompts were refused, so outputs varied on bias.
A February 2023 preprint showing 63% reasoning accuracy. The test dates are not stated and may fall outside the window, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: Release-era evidence shows ChatGPT's outputs varied between acceptable and unacceptable: OpenAI's admission about rephrasing and retries (e1), and the bias outputs that varied (e2). No evidence shows the outputs were consistently right or consistently wrong. The coverage across all seven categories is uneven, but the general claim holds.

attribution.note: Marcus co-wrote the post on his Substack, in the authors' own voice.

semantics.note: 'Can be circumvented' comes from the next sentence of the source. The statement describes guardrails after the December bias patch, and the proposition does not record that time detail.

contract.note: Both sides are required, which is fair to his words. Using launch through the post date as the period is reasonable, though he was strictly describing the guardrails after the patch.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure that the model will sometimes respond to harmful requests: the too-loose side. The surrounding text also expects some false positives.

A launch-day note that cautious training makes the model decline answerable questions. This concerns accuracy trade-offs, not documented guardrail over-refusals, so it is weak for the too-strict side.
Vice, December 1 2022: a fictional-dialogue framing got around the refusal. This is a documented too-loose bypass, though it came before the patch.
CNBC, published February 2023: the DAN role-play jailbreak dates from December 2022. This supports the too-loose side within the period.

reviews.rationale: The 'imperfect' and 'too loose' parts hold: bypasses through indirect framing are documented (e3, e4) and OpenAI admits them (e1). The 'too strict' part rests only on OpenAI's general note on cautious training. The packet has no dated example of an absurdly over-cautious refusal, so that part is unresolved.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps both parts and ties 'when released' to the bias part.

contract.note: Documented fabrications and biased outputs in the launch window is a fair, ordinary reading.

evidence.note: OpenAI's launch disclosure admits plausible-sounding but incorrect answers. It is a company statement, but it admits a weakness.
The Register, December 5 2022: false biographical information and bad math stated as fact, and Stack Overflow reported high error rates.
Daily Beast via Yahoo, December 2022: Piantadosi documented racist and sexist outputs within days of release.

reviews.rationale: Contemporaneous reports (e2, e3) and OpenAI's own launch disclosure (e1) show that launch-era ChatGPT stated false information as fact and produced racist and sexist outputs. The packet contains no counterevidence.
